errors.problem: The entry says the court of appeals 'reversed' the summary judgment and that the Supreme Court 'reversed that approach.' The D.C. Circuit affirmed summary judgment as to 21 of the 30 challenged statements and reversed only as to 9, and the Supreme Court vacated (not reversed) that judgment and remanded.
errors.correction: The district court granted summary judgment on all thirty statements. The D.C. Circuit affirmed as to twenty-one but reversed as to nine, holding that the clear-and-convincing standard need not be applied at the summary-judgment stage. The Supreme Court (White, J., 6-3) vacated that judgment and remanded, holding that the substantive evidentiary standard governs the Rule 56 inquiry.

errors.problem: The entry says Justice Scalia 'wrote for four Justices.' Scalia's opinion was joined in full only by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justice Kennedy; Justice White joined only Parts I, II-A, II-B and II-C, not the part answering Brennan (II-D).
errors.correction: Justice Scalia announced the judgment in an opinion joined in full by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justice Kennedy, and by Justice White except for Part II-D. Justice Brennan concurred in the judgment for four Justices (Brennan, Marshall, Blackmun, O'Connor). Justice White and Justice Stevens each wrote separately concurring in the judgment; Stevens declined to join either main opinion.

errors.problem: Says the Supreme Court 'reversed that allocation'. The district court's allocation had already been reversed by the Second Circuit; the Supreme Court's disposition was to vacate the Second Circuit's judgment and remand with directions to dismiss the class action as defined (the Court also reviewed appellate jurisdiction under the collateral-order doctrine).
errors.correction: The district court, after a preliminary merits hearing, ordered defendants to pay 90 percent of the notice cost; the Second Circuit reversed and ordered the class action dismissed. The Supreme Court (Powell, J.) agreed that Rule 23 authorizes neither a preliminary merits inquiry nor shifting notice costs to defendants, vacated the Second Circuit's judgment and remanded with directions to dismiss the class action as then defined.

errors.problem: Left blank; the decision was not unanimous.
errors.correction: Justice Douglas, joined by Justices Brennan and Marshall, dissented in part, arguing that the district court should be allowed to define smaller, manageable subclasses rather than being forced to require individual notice to all 2.25 million identifiable members.

errors.problem: Says only that the lower courts dismissed the suit; the actual ground was a jurisdictional one, not pleading insufficiency, and the entry does not say that the Supreme Court reversed.
errors.correction: The district court dismissed on the ground that the National Railroad Adjustment Board had exclusive jurisdiction, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed. The Supreme Court (Black, J., unanimous) reversed, rejecting the Adjustment Board argument, the argument that the railroad was an indispensable party, and the argument that the complaint lacked specific facts.

errors.problem: Names the dissenting judge as Judge Edwards.
errors.correction: Senior Circuit Judge McAllister dissented from the Sixth Circuit's expansive treatment of the counterclaims and cross-claims (the panel was Judges Phillips, who wrote the majority opinion, Celebrezze, and McAllister).

errors.problem: The entry says the Supreme Court 'vacated and remanded'. The Court reversed the Third Circuit's judgment (unanimous opinion by Justice Harlan) and remanded for consideration of the issues the court of appeals had not reached.
errors.correction: The Supreme Court, in a unanimous opinion by Justice Harlan, reversed the Third Circuit's judgment and remanded for consideration of the insurer's remaining merits arguments.

errors.problem: The entry says Justice Holmes's dissent was joined by Justice Brandeis. Justice McReynolds, not Brandeis, concurred in Holmes's dissent; Justice Day wrote the majority.
errors.correction: Justice Holmes dissented, joined by Justice McReynolds, arguing that a suit arises under the law that creates the cause of action, which here was Missouri law.

errors.problem: The entry's description ('Separate views questioned the weight given to the American manufacturing issues') does not match the actual separate opinions. Justice Marshall wrote for the Court; Justice White concurred in part and dissented in part; Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Brennan, dissented on the ground that the Court should have vacated and remanded so the Third Circuit could reconsider the district court's discretionary balancing under the correct change-of-law rule; Justices Powell and O'Connor did not participate.
errors.correction: Justice Marshall wrote for the Court. Justice White concurred in part and dissented in part, and Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Brennan, dissented, agreeing that an unfavorable change in law is not dispositive but arguing the Court should have vacated and remanded for the Third Circuit to review the district court's balancing. Justices Powell and O'Connor took no part.

errors.problem: Lists only Justice Thomas's dissent (joined by three Justices). There was a second dissent: Justice Kagan filed a separate dissenting opinion, joined by Justices Breyer and Sotomayor.
errors.correction: Justice Thomas, joined by Justices Breyer, Sotomayor, and Kagan, dissented, arguing that a violation of an individualized private right created by Congress has historically sufficed as injury in fact. Justice Kagan, joined by Justices Breyer and Sotomayor, also filed a separate dissent. The majority opinion was by Justice Kavanaugh for a 5–4 Court.

errors.problem: The field is empty, but the decision was 6–3 with a written dissent.
errors.correction: Justice Jackson, joined by Justices Rutledge and Burton, dissented, arguing that the Court's refusal to accept the state court's own reading of the effect of its statute (unenforceable in state court, not void) was a perversion of the Erie doctrine.

errors.problem: The procedure omits the lower-court posture and the disposition: it reads as if the Supreme Court simply required deference, without saying what it reversed.
errors.correction: The district court granted summary judgment for the defendant and dismissed with prejudice, holding the contract void under Mississippi law. The Fifth Circuit reversed, reading Mississippi law as making the contract merely unenforceable in Mississippi courts rather than void. The Supreme Court (Douglas, J., 6–3) reversed the Fifth Circuit, holding that under Erie the summary judgment was properly granted.

errors.problem: Says the appellate court 'upheld the requirement' without stating the actual disposition; it reads as an affirmance. The plaintiff had won a verdict below and the appellate court reversed.
errors.correction: The plaintiff recovered a judgment after the trial court admitted evidence of the shoulder injury and increased blood pressure over objection. The Missouri Court of Appeals (St. Louis) reversed and remanded for a new trial on both liability and damages, holding that special damages must be specifically pleaded even though the defendant's insurer had actual notice of the conditions.

errors.problem: The entry lists no separate opinions, but the June 30, 2021 decision was not unanimous: Justice Dougherty filed a concurring and dissenting opinion and former Chief Justice Saylor dissented.
errors.correction: Justice Wecht wrote for the majority. Justice Dougherty filed a concurring and dissenting opinion, and former Chief Justice Saylor dissented, disagreeing that Castor's press release should produce the majority's result and preferring the narrower remedy of suppressing the evidence derived from the civil depositions rather than barring retrial.

errors.problem: The entry gives the contract amount as $530,724.14; the case-brief snippet (Quimbee-derived) gives $530,742.14. One of the two transposes digits; the $14,070 deduction and 67-day delay match.
errors.correction: The commission deducted $14,070 from the $530,742.14 contract amount (verify the figure against the printed opinion, 156 N.W.2d 185).

errors.problem: The entry dates the four Scissor-Tail contracts to a 1978 concert tour. The contracts for the Leon Russell concerts were made in 1973 (the arbitration and confirmation followed later in the decade; the Supreme Court decided the case in 1981).
errors.correction: Graham and Scissor-Tail entered four contracts in 1973 for concerts by Leon Russell, on the American Federation of Musicians' standard form.

errors.problem: The entry says 'The King's Bench directed entry of the defendants' verdict.' The case was decided in 1863, during Queen Victoria's reign, by the Court of Queen's Bench (Blackburn J.), not the King's Bench.
errors.correction: A verdict was initially returned for the organizers with leave reserved to enter a verdict for the defendants. The Court of Queen's Bench (Blackburn J., 6 May 1863) directed entry of the defendants' verdict.

errors.problem: Says 'the four dissenters also rejected the plurality's theory.' Only three Justices dissented outright (Douglas, Brennan, Marshall); Justice White concurred in part and dissented in part. Rehnquist's plurality was joined only by Burger and Stewart.
errors.correction: Rehnquist announced the judgment in an opinion joined only by Burger and Stewart. Powell (joined by Blackmun) concurred in part and in the result, White concurred in part and dissented in part, and Marshall (joined by Douglas and Brennan) dissented, with Douglas adding a separate dissent; six Justices thus rejected the plurality's theory even though the judgment upholding the procedures was 6-3.

errors.problem: Says the captain seized a vessel traveling from France to the United States.
errors.correction: Captain Little seized the Flying Fish, a Danish brigantine, near Hispaniola on suspicion that she was American, while she was sailing from Jérémie (a French port) to the Danish island of St. Thomas. The Nonintercourse Act authorized seizure only of American vessels bound to French ports, while the President's instructions had extended seizures to vessels sailing from French ports.

errors.problem: The entry says 'A divided D.C. Circuit set it aside.' In Chenery I the court of appeals affirmed the SEC's order (128 F.2d 303 (D.C. Cir. 1942)); it was the Supreme Court that reversed.
errors.correction: The managers petitioned for review and the court of appeals affirmed the SEC's order, 128 F.2d 303 (D.C. Cir. 1942). The Supreme Court granted certiorari and reversed, holding that the order could not stand on the grounds the Commission had stated. Frankfurter wrote; Black dissented joined by Reed and Murphy; Douglas took no part.

errors.problem: The entry describes 'separate concurrences by Souter and Ginsburg' and omits the lower-court ruling and disposition. There was one concurrence in the judgment by Souter, joined by Ginsburg; the district court had held the members had standing and struck down the Act, and the Supreme Court vacated with instructions to dismiss.
errors.correction: The District Court for the District of Columbia held that the members had standing and that the Line Item Veto Act was unconstitutional; on direct expedited appeal the Supreme Court (Rehnquist, C.J., 7-2 in the judgment) vacated and remanded with instructions to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction. Souter, joined by Ginsburg, concurred in the judgment; Stevens and Breyer each dissented.

errors.problem: Entry dates Taft's withdrawal order to 1910; the Midwest Oil withdrawal (Petroleum Withdrawal No. 5) was issued September 27, 1909, and Midwest Oil's entry on the land was in March 1910 (the Pickett Act followed in June 1910). The 'international tension' motive is also doubtful; the stated concern was that the Navy would soon have to buy back oil from lands the government had given away.
Entry omits that the decision was 5-3 with Justice Day dissenting, joined by McKenna and Van Devanter (McReynolds not participating); a note account, so omission is not an error.

errors.what: Scalia wrote for a unanimous Court on the cost question; Thomas concurred (questioning the intelligible-principle test itself), Stevens concurred in part (joined by Souter, arguing the delegated power is legislative but permissible), and Breyer concurred in part on the cost question. The opinion also contains the well-known line that Congress 'does not, one might say, hide elephants in mouseholes.'
The Supreme Court later adopted the same domestic-only reading of 'convicted in any court' in Small v. United States (2005).
Roberts wrote for a 6-3 Court; Gorsuch concurred (joined by Alito) setting out a framework for the major questions doctrine; Kagan dissented, joined by Breyer and Sotomayor.

Black wrote for the Court; Frankfurter, Douglas, Jackson, Burton and Clark each concurred separately (Jackson's three-category framework is the one usually cited); Chief Justice Vinson dissented, joined by Reed and Minton. The district court had enjoined the seizure and the Supreme Court affirmed.

2011; Scalia for a unanimous 8-0 Court (Kagan recused); the district court granted summary judgment to the employer and the en banc Sixth Circuit affirmed; the Supreme Court reversed. Ginsburg concurred, joined by Breyer.

2023, 8-1: Kavanaugh wrote for five (Roberts, Sotomayor, Kagan, Jackson); Gorsuch concurred in the judgment joined by Thomas and Barrett; Barrett also concurred in the judgment joined by Gorsuch; Alito dissented. The Court reversed the district court's vacatur of the enforcement-priorities guidance.
Frankfurter's familiar formulation: 'The substantiality of evidence must take into account whatever in the record fairly detracts from its weight.'
Rehnquist wrote for the Court; the district court was a three-judge court; the Supreme Court reversed.

Stone wrote for the Court, 6-3; Roberts dissented and Rutledge dissented joined by Murphy (the dissents concerned the bar on challenging regulations in enforcement prosecutions rather than the delegation).

errors.problem: Cannot be checked at all from the checker's knowledge (decision postdates reliable knowledge); vote, author, quotation and date must be verified against the slip opinion.

additions.what: Whitchurch had worked for A.F.A. as a tour escort for about seventeen years and had escorted roughly 1,500 A.F.A. clients; the district court raised the jurisdictional amount on its own at the close of argument and granted summary judgment for Whitchurch, and the Second Circuit vacated under the rule that the sum claimed by the plaintiff controls if made in good faith unless it appears to a legal certainty that the claim is for less.

The Concepcions were charged $30.22 in sales tax on phones advertised as free; the district court denied AT&T's motion to compel arbitration under California's Discover Bank rule and the Ninth Circuit affirmed; the Supreme Court (Scalia, J., 5-4) reversed and remanded, with Justice Thomas concurring and Justice Breyer's dissent joined by Justices Ginsburg, Sotomayor and Kagan.

Justice Harlan wrote for the Court; the case is the source of the rule that the party moving for summary judgment bears the burden of showing the absence of a genuine issue of material fact, so Kress had to foreclose the possibility that a policeman was in the store, and Adickes's first count (refusal of service under a custom of segregation) went to trial and ended in a directed verdict for Kress that the Court also reversed.

Aldinger was a clerk in the Spokane County treasurer's office who was fired without a hearing for living with her boyfriend; she sued the treasurer under section 1983 and joined Spokane County on a state-law claim, and the Court (Rehnquist, J.) held that Congress's then-understood exclusion of counties from section 1983 barred pendent-party jurisdiction over the county, a result later addressed by Monell (1978) and by 28 U.S.C. section 1367(a).

Justice Ginsburg wrote for the Court (6-2, Justice O'Connor not participating); the opinion holds that settlement is relevant to certification because a court need not consider trial-manageability problems, but the other Rule 23 requirements demand undiluted, even heightened, attention in the settlement context, and that predominance is far more demanding than Rule 23(a)(2) commonality.

American Well Works sued in Arkansas state court for slander of its patented pump; Layne removed, the district court dismissed on the theory that the suit arose under patent law, and the Supreme Court (Holmes, J., with Justice McKenna dissenting) reversed, stating the creation test: a suit arises under the law that creates the cause of action.

Justice White wrote for a 6-3 Court; Justice Brennan dissented, and Justice Rehnquist dissented joined by Chief Justice Burger, both objecting to importing the trial-stage clear-and-convincing standard into Rule 56. The plaintiffs were Liberty Lobby and its founder Willis Carto, suing columnist Jack Anderson over articles in The Investigator magazine, and the opinion is also the source of the rule that a mere scintilla of evidence is insufficient to defeat summary judgment.

Ira Arnstein sued Cole Porter claiming Porter had plagiarized his compositions (including 'Night and Day' and 'Begin the Beguine'); the district court granted Porter summary judgment, and the Second Circuit (Frank, J.) reversed and remanded because Porter's denial of access was not 'indubitable' and his credibility should be tested by cross-examination at trial, over Judge Clark's dissent calling the claim fantastic and trial a waste.

The case began with Gary Zurcher's motorcycle accident; Cheng Shin (Taiwan) impleaded Asahi (Japan), and Justice O'Connor's Part II-A plurality (joined by Rehnquist, Powell and Scalia) required 'additional conduct' directed at the forum beyond awareness, giving as examples designing the product for the forum market, advertising there, establishing channels for advice to forum customers, or marketing through a distributor who agreed to sell in the forum; Justice Brennan's four-Justice group would have found awareness that the product regularly reaches the forum sufficient.

Justice Kennedy wrote for a 5-4 Court; the defendants were Attorney General Ashcroft and FBI Director Mueller, the case reached the Court on interlocutory appeal from the denial of qualified immunity, and the opinion sets out the two-step method: disregard conclusory allegations not entitled to the assumption of truth, then ask whether the remaining well-pleaded facts plausibly (not merely possibly) give rise to an entitlement to relief.

The decision was unanimous (Alito, J.); the district court had denied both the motion to dismiss and the alternative section 1404(a) transfer motion and the Fifth Circuit denied mandamus. Under the modified section 1404(a) analysis the plaintiff's choice of forum merits no weight, the private-interest factors are treated as weighing entirely in favor of the preselected forum, and the transferee court does not carry over the original forum's choice-of-law rules; a valid clause should be given controlling weight in all but the most exceptional cases.

Justice Ginsburg wrote for an 8-1 Court reversing the Montana Supreme Court; the plaintiffs were Robert Nelson (injured in his work as a fuel-truck driver) and Kelli Tyrrell (widow of an employee who died of cancer allegedly from chemical exposure), BNSF is incorporated in Delaware with its principal place of business in Texas, and its roughly 2,000 miles of Montana track was about 6 percent of its total; the Court also held that FELA section 56 is a venue and concurrent-jurisdiction provision, not a grant of personal jurisdiction.

Sara Boyd died in 1937 leaving an estate of about $225,000; her niece Bertha Smedley sued to enforce Boyd's alleged contract to leave her the entire estate, serving only the Bank of California (executor) and St. Luke's Hospital (the residuary legatee), and the court distinguished 'necessary' parties, who should be joined if possible, from 'indispensable' parties, without whom the action cannot proceed at all.

Bates incurred the debt while living in the Western District of Pennsylvania and C & S was a local Pennsylvania collection agency doing no regular business in New York; the Postal Service forwarded the unmarked notice to Bates's new Western District of New York address, and the Second Circuit reversed and remanded under the 1990 amendment to 28 U.S.C. section 1391 (a district where a substantial part of the events giving rise to the claim occurred), reasoning that the harm from an abusive collection notice occurs on receipt.

Aquaslide's original admission of manufacture rested on inspections by three insurance investigators; its president and owner Carl Meyer later inspected the slide himself before his deposition and concluded it was a counterfeit, and the Eighth Circuit affirmed under Rule 15(a) because the plaintiffs had not shown bad faith and might still have remedies against the actual manufacturer.

Justice Souter wrote for a 7-2 Court; the plaintiffs were subscribers of local telephone and high-speed internet service suing the incumbent local exchange carriers under section 1 of the Sherman Act, and the opinion retired Conley v. Gibson's 'no set of facts' formulation, requiring instead enough facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face; Justice Ginsburg joined the Stevens dissent except as to Part IV.

Justice Holmes dissented, joined by Justices Brandeis and Stone, arguing that the common law enforced in a state is the law of that state existing by its authority and that the Swift doctrine was an unconstitutional assumption of power by the federal courts; the majority (Butler, J., 6-3) upheld the exclusive contract with the Louisville & Nashville Railroad for the Bowling Green, Kentucky station after the Kentucky owners reincorporated in Tennessee and dissolved the Kentucky company.

Justice Scalia wrote for a 5-4 Court; Boyle's estate brought a diversity action under Virginia law against Sikorsky (a division of United Technologies), won a $725,000 jury verdict, the Fourth Circuit reversed and directed judgment for Sikorsky, and the Supreme Court vacated and remanded for application of the three-part test; Justice Brennan's dissent was joined by Justices Marshall and Blackmun.

Bright filed a W-4 claiming exemption from federal income-tax withholding and then sued in California state court for breach of contract when Bechtel withheld anyway; Bechtel removed, the district court denied remand, dismissed, and awarded attorney's fees, and the Ninth Circuit affirmed and imposed sanctions for a frivolous appeal, invoking the artful-pleading doctrine as a limit on the plaintiff's status as master of the complaint.

The product was Wesson cooking oil labeled '100% Natural,' allegedly misleading because it contained genetically modified ingredients; the Ninth Circuit sided with the Sixth, Seventh and Eighth Circuits against the Third Circuit's administrative-feasibility requirement, reasoning that such a rule would effectively bar class actions over inexpensive consumer goods where no one keeps receipts.

Justice Alito wrote for an 8-1 Court; the plaintiffs were 86 California residents and 592 residents of 33 other states, BMS is incorporated in Delaware and headquartered in New York, and the Court rejected the California Supreme Court's 'sliding scale' approach, requiring a connection between the forum and the specific claims at issue while leaving open whether the Fifth Amendment imposes the same limits on federal courts.

Justice Brennan wrote for a 6-2 Court (Justice Powell not participating) reversing the Eleventh Circuit; the opinion states that contacts must not be random, fortuitous or attenuated, that a contract alone does not automatically establish minimum contacts, and that courts look to prior negotiations, contemplated future consequences, the contract's terms and the parties' actual course of dealing; Rudzewicz's co-franchisee MacShara attended Burger King's management course in Miami.

Dennis Burnham was a New Jersey resident served with his estranged wife's California divorce petition during a three-day visit; the Scalia opinion reasons that jurisdiction based on physical presence alone satisfies due process because it is one of the continuing traditions of our legal system, while Brennan's concurrence reasons that a visitor knowingly avails himself of the state's benefits and protections and can reasonably anticipate being sued there.

Justice Brennan wrote for the Court; Byrd, a North Carolina resident, won a jury verdict against the South Carolina cooperative, the Fourth Circuit reversed and directed judgment for the cooperative, and the Supreme Court reversed and remanded for a new trial; Justices Frankfurter and Harlan dissented. The opinion describes the federal jury allocation as reflecting the influence, if not the command, of the Seventh Amendment.

The decision was unanimous (Rehnquist, J.); the defendants were National Enquirer reporter John South and president-editor Iain Calder, the Enquirer sold over 600,000 copies a week in California out of about 5,000,000 nationally, and the Court held that First Amendment concerns play no role in the jurisdictional analysis and that the defendants were not mere employees whose contacts are judged by the employer's.

Justice Blackmun wrote for a 7-2 Court; the Ninth Circuit had found specific jurisdiction in Washington under a 'but for' test tied to Carnival's solicitation there and refused to enforce the clause under Bremen v. Zapata because it was not freely bargained, and the Court reasoned that a cruise line's clause serves legitimate interests by dispelling confusion about where suits may be brought, sparing litigation over the forum, and reducing fares.

Justice Rehnquist wrote for a 5-4 Court (joined by White, Marshall, Powell and O'Connor); the opinion describes summary judgment as an integral part of the Federal Rules rather than a disfavored procedural shortcut, and Justice White's concurrence stressed that a movant cannot simply assert that the opponent has no evidence and must still support its motion.

Justice Douglas wrote for the Court; a 1936 WPA check payable to Clair Barner was stolen, forged and cashed at a J. C. Penney store in Clearfield, Pennsylvania, the district court applied Pennsylvania law and ruled for the bank on the government's delay, the Third Circuit reversed, and the Supreme Court affirmed, holding that the rights and duties of the United States on its own commercial paper are governed by federal law fashioned by the federal courts, since applying varying state rules would create uncertainty for a nationwide program.

Justice Jackson wrote for the Court; the district court denied the corporation's motion to require security, the Third Circuit reversed, and the Supreme Court affirmed. The case is also the origin of the collateral-order doctrine: the order was immediately appealable because it conclusively determined a question separate from the merits that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment; the New Jersey statute, enacted in 1945 while the action was pending, applied to holders of less than 5 percent (or $50,000) of the stock.

The action was one of trespass on the case in the federal circuit court for North Carolina; the record alleged only that Van Noorden was 'late of Pitt County' and said nothing about Capron's own citizenship, and the plaintiff who had lost on the merits successfully used the jurisdictional defect he himself had failed to plead to obtain reversal.

The opinion's famous (and since retired) standard: "a complaint should not be dismissed for failure to state a claim unless it appears beyond doubt that the plaintiff can prove no set of facts in support of his claim which would entitle him to relief"; Bell Atlantic v. Twombly (2007) declared this 'no set of facts' language to have earned its retirement.

The union, Local 28 of the Brotherhood of Railway and Steamship Clerks, allegedly acquiesced in the Texas and New Orleans Railroad's May 1954 discharge of 45 Black employees who were then replaced by white workers, and ignored the members' repeated requests for help.

John DiGiovanni sued Brian Doehr for assault and battery and, on a one-page affidavit, obtained an ex parte $75,000 attachment on Doehr's home under a Connecticut statute that required no bond and no pre-attachment notice.

Justice White wrote; Parts I–III (applying the Mathews v. Eldridge factors, adapted to a private-creditor dispute, and holding the statute unconstitutional) spoke for the Court, while Part IV (that due process would also require a bond) was joined only by Justices Marshall, Stevens and O'Connor; Chief Justice Rehnquist (joined by Justice Blackmun) and Justice Scalia concurred in part and in the judgment.

The class suit was originally an EEOC action (filed March 1977) in which Cooper and three other employees intervened and won certification of a class of Black employees; the district court found a pattern of discrimination only in pay grades 4 and 5, and the Baxter plaintiffs (who had received notice and not opted out) then filed separate individual promotion claims.

Justice Stevens wrote for a unanimous Court: a class judgment on a pattern-or-practice claim precludes relitigation of whether the employer engaged in a pattern of discrimination, but does not bar individual class members from proving discrete individual claims in later suits.

Procedural history: the Northern District of California dismissed for want of personal jurisdiction; a Ninth Circuit panel first affirmed, then on rehearing reversed and upheld jurisdiction (with en banc rehearing denied); the Supreme Court (Ginsburg, J.) reversed the Ninth Circuit.

Rule statement: a corporation is 'at home' for general jurisdiction in its place of incorporation and its principal place of business, and only in an exceptional case elsewhere; the plaintiffs were Argentine residents suing over Mercedes-Benz Argentina's alleged collaboration with state security forces during the 'Dirty War'.

Facts and posture: Owens filed a Kansas state-court class action over underpaid oil-and-gas royalties; Dart's CAFA removal notice alleged more than $8 million in controversy without evidence; the district court remanded under Tenth Circuit precedent, the Tenth Circuit denied leave to appeal the remand, and the Supreme Court (Ginsburg, J.) held that denial an abuse of discretion, vacated and remanded.

The Court also stated that no antiremoval presumption attends cases invoking CAFA, and that when the amount is contested the removing defendant must establish it by a preponderance of the evidence under 28 U.S.C. § 1446(c)(2)(B).

The decision was 5–4: Justice Scalia dissented (joined by Justices Kennedy and Kagan, and by Justice Thomas in part) on the ground that the Court could review only the Tenth Circuit's discretionary refusal to hear the appeal, and Justice Thomas dissented separately.

Dice, a railroad fireman, alleged the railroad told him the release was merely a receipt for back pay; the trial court entered judgment notwithstanding the jury's verdict, the Ohio Court of Appeals reversed, the Ohio Supreme Court reinstated judgment for the railroad, and the U.S. Supreme Court (Black, J.) reversed.

Justice Frankfurter's separate opinion, joined by Justices Reed, Jackson and Burton, concurred in reversal on the release question but dissented from requiring the state court to send the fraud issue to the jury.

The opinion was written by Judge Charles E. Clark, the principal draftsman of the Federal Rules; the 'home-drawn' complaint alleged that the customs collector sold the tonics at auction to another bidder for $10 less than Dioguardi's own bid and that two cases had disappeared three weeks before the sale.

Judge Learned Hand wrote for the Second Circuit; the alleged slander was that MacDougall said Dyer had sent a 'blackmailing letter' to Queensboro Corporation shareholders, and all four alleged speakers and hearers denied the statements by affidavit or deposition, leaving Dyer no witness to prove the utterance.

The Court also held that Rule 23(c)(2) requires individual notice to every class member who can be identified through reasonable effort (about 2,250,000 of the roughly six million odd-lot traders), and that 'nothing in either the language or history of Rule 23' authorizes a preliminary inquiry into the merits when deciding certification.

The Kansas Supreme Court held that an insured fully paid by its insurer (Potomac Insurance Co.) is not the real party in interest under the Kansas code and cannot sue in its own name 'for the use and benefit of' the insurer; the result would differ for partial subrogation, where insured and insurer each hold part of the claim.

Tompkins, a Pennsylvania citizen, was struck by something protruding from a passing Erie train while walking on a footpath beside the tracks at night, and sued in the Southern District of New York (Erie being a New York corporation); Justice Brandeis wrote for the Court, declaring that there is no federal general common law.
Vote detail: Justice Reed concurred in part (statutory ground only); Justice Butler dissented, joined by Justice McReynolds; Justice Cardozo did not participate.

The two consolidated cases were the Exxon dealers' class action (about 10,000 dealers alleging fuel overcharges, where the Eleventh Circuit upheld supplemental jurisdiction after a jury verdict) and Ortega v. Star-Kist (a nine-year-old injured by a tuna can, where only her claim met the amount and the First Circuit rejected jurisdiction over her family's claims); the Court (Kennedy, J.) affirmed the Eleventh Circuit and reversed the First Circuit.

The majority distinguished incomplete diversity, which 'contaminates' the whole action and so is not cured by § 1367, from a single plaintiff's failure to meet the amount in controversy, which does not.

Facts and posture: Finley's husband and children died when their plane struck power lines approaching a San Diego airfield; she sued the United States under the FTCA for FAA negligence, then moved to add state-law claims against the City of San Diego and the utility; the district court allowed it under Gibbs, the Ninth Circuit reversed, and the Supreme Court (Scalia, J.) affirmed.
The decision was 5–4: Justice Blackmun dissented, and Justice Stevens dissented joined by Justices Brennan and Marshall.

The plaintiffs were the estate of Markkaya Gullett, killed in Montana when a tire on her Ford Explorer failed, and Adam Bandemer, injured in Minnesota as a passenger in a friend's Crown Victoria; Justice Kagan wrote for the Court, which was 8–0 (Justice Barrett not participating).

Rule statement: the 'arise out of or relate to' formulation has two halves; the first asks about causation, but the second contemplates that some relationships will support jurisdiction without a causal showing, though 'relate to' incorporates real limits.

Margarita Fuentes bought a gas stove and a stereo from Firestone on conditional sales contracts; after a dispute over servicing she stopped paying with about $200 left, and a sheriff seized the goods on a writ obtained from a court clerk on a double-value bond before she had even received the summons.
Justice Stewart wrote for a 4–3 Court; Justice White dissented, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Blackmun; Justices Powell and Rehnquist did not participate.

Garcia, a Puerto Rico resident, sued the Delaware hotel corporation after being 'violently discharged' amid accusations of bringing prostitution to the hotel; the case was removed to the federal court for Puerto Rico, which held that a conditional (qualified) privilege is a defense the defendant must prove and cannot support dismissal, whereas statements at the labor-department hearing were absolutely privileged.

Gasperini, a journalist, had lent 300 original slide transparencies that the Center lost; the jury awarded $1,500 per slide, the district court denied a new trial, and the Second Circuit ordered a new trial unless he accepted a remittitur to $100,000; the Supreme Court (Ginsburg, J., 5–4) vacated and remanded for the district judge to apply New York's 'deviates materially' standard.

The complaint alleged that on May 5 and 6, 1959 in Alamance County the defendants trespassed on her premises, assaulted her, and had her seized, exhibited as a prisoner and jailed; four groups of defendants demurred, the trial court sustained each demurrer, and the North Carolina Supreme Court affirmed because the pleading failed to say what occurred, when, where, and who did what.

Two 13-year-old boys from North Carolina died in a bus crash outside Paris attributed to a tire made in Turkey; the defendants were Goodyear USA and its subsidiaries in Turkey, France and Luxembourg, and Justice Ginsburg wrote for a unanimous Court, framing the paradigm general-jurisdiction forums as the place of incorporation and the principal place of business.

The IRS seized Grable's Michigan property in 1994 for unpaid taxes and sold it to Darue after certified-mail notice; five years later Grable sued to quiet title, and the Sixth Circuit affirmed federal jurisdiction before the Supreme Court (Souter, J., unanimous) did so, clarifying that Merrell Dow's absence of a federal private right of action is a factor, not a bar.
Justice Thomas concurred, suggesting he would be open in a future case to returning to Justice Holmes's test that a suit arises under the law that creates the cause of action.

Phyllis Gray was injured in Cook County when the water heater exploded; Titan sold its valves to American Radiator in Pennsylvania, which built them into heaters; the circuit court dismissed both Gray's complaint and American Radiator's cross-claim against Titan, and the appeal went directly to the Illinois Supreme Court because it raised a constitutional question about substituted service on nonresidents.

Guaranty Trust was indenture trustee for $30 million of Van Sweringen Corporation notes; York, who received her notes by gift in 1934 and declined the exchange offer after default, sued in a diversity class action for breach of trust; Justice Frankfurter wrote the 'outcome-determinative' opinion, and Justice Rutledge dissented, joined by Justice Murphy.

Minton's TEXCEN trading-software patent was invalidated under the on-sale bar because he had leased the system more than a year before applying; Chief Justice Roberts wrote for a unanimous Court, restating the Grable inquiry as whether the federal issue is (1) necessarily raised, (2) actually disputed, (3) substantial, and (4) capable of federal resolution without disrupting the federal-state balance approved by Congress.

Hadges, a harness-racing driver whose license had been suspended and revoked, was represented by William Kunstler; the district court fined Hadges $2,000 and censured Kunstler, partly for failing to disclose a related state-court action, and the Second Circuit reversed because YRC's Rule 11 motion did not comply with the 1993 safe-harbor procedure (service 21 days before filing) and the court imposed sanctions without notice and an opportunity to respond.

Facts: Ethlyn Hall sued her son Samuel over his handling of her Virgin Islands property (the 'trust case'), her daughter Elsa succeeded her as trustee and plaintiff, Samuel sued Elsa individually, and the cases were consolidated under Rule 42(a) and tried together; the Third Circuit dismissed Elsa's appeal from the judgment in the individual case as premature, and the Supreme Court (Roberts, C.J., unanimous) reversed, holding that a final judgment in one consolidated case is immediately appealable.

The Hopkinses leased land to Hancock Oil and Bush Oil in 1936; Independent Distributing later claimed the Hopkinses held the land in trust for it and demanded the $1,500 in accrued landowner royalties; the California Supreme Court held that the lessee's contractual obligation to pay rent is not an 'independent liability' barring interpleader and that the rule against a tenant disputing the landlord's title does not prevent the tenant from interpleading rival claimants.

Hanna, an Ohio citizen, sued Plumer as executor of a Massachusetts decedent's estate over a car accident; Chief Justice Warren wrote for a unanimous Court, reframing York's outcome test by reference to the 'twin aims' of Erie (discouraging forum shopping and avoiding inequitable administration of the laws) and holding that a Federal Rule within the Enabling Act and the Constitution governs regardless of contrary state law.

Carl Hansberry (father of playwright Lorraine Hansberry) bought a home in Chicago's Washington Park in 1937; the covenant required signatures of owners of 95 percent of the frontage but only about 54 percent had signed, and the earlier suit, Burke v. Kleiman, had proceeded on a stipulation that 95 percent had signed; Justice Stone wrote for the Court, reversing the Illinois Supreme Court.

Verbatim rule: 'it is essential in each case that there be some act by which the defendant purposefully avails itself of the privilege of conducting activities within the forum State, thus invoking the benefits and protections of its laws'; the unilateral activity of those claiming a relationship with the defendant cannot supply the contact.

Dora Donner, a Pennsylvanian, created the trust with a Delaware trustee (Wilmington Trust Co.) and later moved to Florida, where she exercised the power of appointment and died; the Court (Warren, C.J., 5–4) held Florida lacked both in rem and in personam jurisdiction, reversed the Florida Supreme Court, and affirmed the Delaware Supreme Court's refusal to give the Florida decree full faith and credit; Justice Black's dissent was joined by Justices Burton and Brennan, and Justice Douglas dissented separately.

Harris demurred for misjoinder; the district court overruled the demurrer and the Kansas Supreme Court affirmed, reading the code to permit joinder of claims arising out of 'the same transaction or transactions connected with the same subject of action' and finding that the accusation, taking of the horse, arrest and four-or-five-day confinement with felons formed one transaction.

The decision was 8-1: Justice Blackmun wrote for the Court and Justice Brennan alone dissented, arguing the Texas contacts were substantial and sufficiently related to the claim; the Court reversed the Texas Supreme Court, which had sustained jurisdiction.

Helicol had bought about 80 percent of its helicopter fleet (roughly $4 million) from Bell Helicopter in Fort Worth, sent pilots and management there for training, and negotiated the Peruvian pipeline contract in Houston; the 1976 crash killed four U.S. citizens whose representatives sued in Texas.

Hess was a Pennsylvania resident sued by Pawloski in Massachusetts state court; the statute deemed driving on Massachusetts highways an appointment of the state registrar of motor vehicles as agent for service, which the Court upheld against a Fourteenth Amendment due-process challenge.

Illinois plaintiffs sued a Texas corporation for patent infringement in Texas; the Texas district court transferred the case to Illinois, and the Seventh Circuit issued mandamus because the defendant could not have been served in Illinois and the action could not have been brought there. The Court held 1404(a) permits transfer only to a district where the plaintiff had a right to bring the action, regardless of defendant consent.
Justice Whittaker wrote the majority; Justice Frankfurter dissented, joined by Justices Harlan and Brennan.

Citibank sued Jackson in North Carolina state court to collect a debt for a water-treatment system; Jackson counterclaimed against Citibank and added class claims against Home Depot and Carolina Water Systems. The Court affirmed the Fourth Circuit 5-4 in an opinion by Justice Thomas (joined by Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor and Kagan), reasoning that a third-party counterclaim defendant is a defendant to a claim but not to the 'civil action.'

The consolidated FTCA cases involved a surgeon's negligent drilling into Ingraham's spine (award of $1,264,000) and a mismanaged cesarean that left Stephanie Bonds brain-damaged (awards of about $3.49 million and $750,000); the cap was the Texas Medical Liability and Insurance Improvement Act, and the court treated it as an 'avoidance' under Rule 8(c) whose purpose is to prevent unfair surprise.

CBG, a Guinean mining company 51 percent owned by Pennsylvania-based Halco, sued in the Western District of Pennsylvania after 21 mostly foreign excess insurers refused a business-interruption claim exceeding $10 million; the Third Circuit affirmed the Rule 37(b)(2)(A) sanction and the Supreme Court affirmed, with Justice White writing and Justice Powell concurring in the judgment.

Chief Justice Stone wrote for the Court (Justice Jackson took no part); the case is the source of the 'minimum contacts' test, and Black's separate opinion warned that the 'fair play' and 'substantial justice' criteria invite the Court to strike down state laws on its own notions of natural justice.

Nicastro injured his hand on a metal-shearing machine made in England by J. McIntyre, which sold in the United States only through an independent Ohio-based exclusive distributor; the Kennedy plurality was joined by Roberts, Scalia and Thomas, and Breyer's concurrence (joined by Alito) rested on the thin record rather than the plurality's sovereignty theory.

The case arose in the District of Minnesota (2 F.R.D. 238, 1942): Jeub got food poisoning from ham at a B/G restaurant, B/G impleaded the manufacturer Swift & Co., and Swift moved to vacate because B/G had suffered no loss yet; the court held Rule 14 reaches a party who 'is or may be liable' and merely accelerates the timing of a Minnesota indemnity right without altering it.

Kearns sued under California's Consumers Legal Remedies Act and Unfair Competition Law; the Ninth Circuit (567 F.3d 1120) affirmed dismissal of his Third Amended Complaint, holding that claims 'grounded in fraud' under those statutes, including nondisclosure claims, must plead the 'who, what, when, where, and how' of the misconduct under Rule 9(b).

Keeton, a New York resident, sued Hustler (an Ohio corporation with its principal place of business in California) in the District of New Hampshire because its six-year libel limitations period was the only one still open; the district court dismissed, the First Circuit affirmed, and the Supreme Court reversed.

Kegerise was the district's fired superintendent; the issue arose on her motion for judgment on the pleadings, where she attacked answers that admitted part of an allegation without denying the rest, labeled allegations 'legal conclusions' requiring no response, and claimed lack of knowledge about matters the defendants knew (M.D. Pa. 2016, 321 F.R.D. 122).

Justice Sotomayor wrote for the Court; Justice Scalia concurred in part, declining to rely on the Advisory Committee Notes. Krupski's ticket named Costa Cruise (the U.S. sales agent) on the front but identified Costa Crociere as carrier on the back; she sued Costa Cruise three weeks before the one-year limitations period ran.

The decision was 6-3: Justice Marshall wrote for the Court and Justice Brennan dissented, joined by Justices White and Powell, concluding the father's California connection was not too attenuated to require him to defend there. The Kulkos had married in California during Ezra's military stopover, lived in New York for 13 years, and signed a separation agreement in New York giving the children to the mother in California for summers and holidays.

LASA (Italian marble supplier) sued subcontractor Alexander, general contractor Southern Builders, its surety Continental Casualty, and the City of Memphis over unpaid marble for the Memphis city hall; Alexander and Southern Builders counterclaimed that LASA shipped the wrong marble late and short, and the Sixth Circuit held the cross-claims and the claim against the architect arose from the same transaction and fell within ancillary jurisdiction.

The husband's divorce judgment (March 1970) was affirmed by the Appellate Division in 1972; two years later the wife moved to vacate it for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because the husband had not met the residence requirement. The Court of Appeals held the residence requirements go to the substance of the cause of action, not the court's competence.

Lexecon sued the Milberg Weiss and Cotchett firms in Illinois for malicious prosecution; the Judicial Panel transferred the case to Arizona for pretrial proceedings, and the Arizona court then transferred it to itself for trial under 1404(a). Justice Souter wrote for a unanimous Court (Justice Scalia did not join Part II-C).

Lively sued in California state court over a slip and fall in a Wild Oats store; Wild Oats removed on diversity, no remand motion was filed within 30 days, and the Ninth Circuit held the forum-defendant rule is procedural and waivable and so cannot support a district court's sua sponte remand, joining eight of nine circuits to decide the question (456 F.3d 933).

Livingston sued former President Jefferson in federal court in Virginia for $100,000, alleging that Jefferson as President had ordered marshals to eject him from land he held in the Territory of Orleans; Marshall (sitting with District Judge Tyler) applied the English local-action rule, so the suit could be brought only in Orleans Territory.

The Mottleys were injured in an 1871 railway accident and settled for lifetime free passes; a 1906 federal act forbade free passes and the railroad refused renewal in 1907. They sought specific performance; the trial court overruled the railroad's demurrer and ruled for them, and the Supreme Court raised the jurisdictional defect on its own motion and directed dismissal.

The vote was 5-4: Gorsuch delivered the opinion of the Court only as to Parts I and III-B (joined by Thomas, Alito, Sotomayor and Jackson), with Parts II, III-A and IV a plurality; Barrett's dissent argued Pennsylvania Fire had been all but overruled by post-International Shoe cases. Mallory's suit was under FELA in a Pennsylvania state court.

Jean Paul Mas (French citizen) and Judy Mas (Mississippi domiciliary) sued their Baton Rouge landlord for invasion of privacy; the jury awarded $5,000 to Mr. Mas and $15,000 to Mrs. Mas. Perry also argued Mr. Mas's $5,000 award fell short of the jurisdictional amount, and the Fifth Circuit rejected that because the claim exceeding the amount was made in good faith.

The decision was 5-4: Justice Powell wrote (joined by Burger, Marshall, Rehnquist and O'Connor) and Justice White dissented, joined by Brennan, Blackmun and Stevens, arguing the majority ignored the DePodwin expert report and weighed evidence that created a genuine issue for trial. The Court required evidence 'that tends to exclude the possibility' that the alleged conspirators acted independently.

Franklin bought the policy in 1944 from Empire Mutual, an Arizona company; International Life, a Texas corporation, assumed its obligations in 1948 and Franklin mailed premiums from California until his death in 1950. McGee, his mother and beneficiary, sued under California's statute permitting service on out-of-state insurers.

Father Reuben Moore filed the custody action; after trial the court orally awarded custody and child support to the mother (with visitation conditioned on a $7,500 bond) and let her file a post-trial counterclaim conforming to the evidence. The D.C. Court of Appeals held custody, child support and attorney's fees were tried by implied consent, but separate maintenance was not because the father lacked notice and an opportunity to contest it.

Ten Black employees sued General Motors and the UAW under Title VII after EEOC reasonable-cause findings; the district court severed the claims into ten separate actions, and the Eighth Circuit (497 F.2d 1330) held that a companywide policy of discrimination is a single series of transactions and that the differing effects on each plaintiff are immaterial to Rule 20 joinder.

Justice Jackson wrote for the Court; Justice Burton dissented, arguing that supplemental notice for state-created common trust funds should be left to state discretion, and Justice Douglas took no part. Mullane was the court-appointed special guardian for beneficiaries who had not appeared, and it was he who objected that publication notice was constitutionally inadequate.

Dr. Florence Mussat, an Illinois physician, sued under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act over two unsolicited junk faxes lacking the required opt-out notice from IQVIA (a Delaware corporation headquartered in Pennsylvania); the Seventh Circuit reasoned that 'absent class members are not full parties to the case' for personal-jurisdiction purposes, and the Supreme Court later denied certiorari.

The Szukhents, a father and son farming in Michigan, leased two incubators from the New York company on a printed form; the decision was 6-3 with Justice Stewart writing, Justice Black dissenting alone, and Justice Brennan dissenting joined by Chief Justice Warren and Justice Goldberg.

The vote was 7-2: Justice Souter wrote for the Court; Chief Justice Rehnquist concurred, joined by Scalia and Kennedy; Justice Breyer dissented, joined by Stevens, arguing the settlement made more money available to more claimants and the Court should have deferred to the district court. The certification was under Rule 23(b)(1)(B), and the Court required that the fund be limited by more than the parties' agreement and allocated through a process addressing conflicting interests.

James Kroger was electrocuted when a crane boom came near a high-tension line in Iowa; his widow sued the Omaha Public Power District (a Nebraska corporation) in diversity, OPPD impleaded Owen under Rule 14, Kroger amended to sue Owen directly, OPPD won summary judgment, and Owen's Iowa principal place of business surfaced only at trial.

Procedurally, the jury returned a verdict for Kroger, the Eighth Circuit affirmed, and the Supreme Court reversed in an opinion by Justice Stewart; Justice White, joined by Justice Brennan, dissented, arguing ancillary jurisdiction should reach the claim because the plaintiff had not tried to evade complete diversity.

Congress codified the Kroger result in 28 U.S.C. § 1367(b), which withholds supplemental jurisdiction in diversity cases over claims by plaintiffs against persons made parties under Rules 14, 19, 20 or 24 when that would be inconsistent with § 1332.

The case arose in the Eastern District of Louisiana (Judge J. Skelly Wright) from a collision between a tractor-trailer and a school bus near Covington, Louisiana; the insurer deposited a $100,000 bond equal to its policy limit, and the court enjoined all claimants from suing elsewhere, required claims to be filed within 30 days, and ordered a joint trial on liability and damages.

Mitchell was an Oregon attorney suing for roughly $300 in unpaid legal fees; he bought Neff's land himself at the sheriff's sale and then conveyed it to Pennoyer, and Justice Field wrote the majority opinion.

Pennoyer's famous rule: every state possesses exclusive jurisdiction over persons and property within its territory and none may exercise direct jurisdiction over persons or property outside it, so a personal judgment against a nonresident who was neither served in the state nor appeared is void.

Perkins, herself a nonresident of Ohio, sued for dividends and stock certificates; the company's president ran the business from Ohio during the Japanese occupation of the Philippines (directors' meetings, correspondence, banking, stock transfers, salaries, purchases), and the Court described these as 'continuous and systematic' activities supporting jurisdiction on a claim that did not arise in Ohio.
The Ohio courts had refused jurisdiction; the Supreme Court vacated and remanded, holding that due process neither compelled nor forbade Ohio to hear the case, leaving the choice to Ohio.

Justice Rehnquist wrote for the Court; the class of roughly 33,000 royalty owners spanned all fifty states, and about 99% of the leases and 97% of the class members had no Kansas connection other than the suit; it was the defendant, Phillips, that raised the absent class members' due-process objection, and the Court allowed it standing to do so.

Rule statement: an absent plaintiff class member is bound if given adequate notice, an opportunity to be heard, a right to opt out, and adequate representation, so minimum contacts with the forum are not required; but a forum may apply its own law only if it has a significant contact or aggregation of contacts creating state interests, so the choice of law is not arbitrary or unfair.

The 1976 crash killed the pilot and five Scottish passengers; Piper built the plane in Pennsylvania and Hartzell Propeller built the propeller in Ohio; Gaynell Reyno, a California legal secretary appointed administratrix, filed in California state court, and the case was removed and then transferred under § 1404(a) to the Middle District of Pennsylvania.

Rule statements: a foreign plaintiff's choice of a United States forum deserves less deference than a resident's, and an unfavorable change in law may be given substantial weight only where the alternative forum's remedy is so clearly inadequate or unsatisfactory that it is no remedy at all; the district court's balancing of the Gilbert private- and public-interest factors is reviewed for abuse of discretion.

Poller owned WCAN, a UHF station in Milwaukee; he alleged CBS conspired to cancel WCAN's network affiliation, acquire competing station WOKY, and buy WCAN's equipment at distressed prices, in a treble-damage Sherman Act suit.

The decision was 5-4: Justice Clark wrote for the Court, and Justice Harlan dissented, joined by Justices Frankfurter, Whittaker and Stewart; the majority's oft-quoted rationale is that summary procedures should be used sparingly in complex antitrust cases where motive and intent play leading roles, the proof is largely in the hands of the alleged conspirators, and hostile witnesses thicken the plot.

The insurer, Lumbermens Mutual Casualty Co., had refused to defend on the theory that Cionci lacked Dutcher's permission; Provident Tradesmens Bank, administrator of passenger Lynch's estate, sought a declaratory judgment that Cionci was a permitted user covered by the policy, and the jury found for the plaintiffs.

The Court identified four interests for the Rule 19(b) inquiry: the plaintiff's interest in a forum, the defendant's interest in avoiding multiple or inconsistent liability, the absent person's interest, and the public and the courts' interest in complete, consistent and efficient settlement of controversies; and it stressed that after a judgment has been rendered the balance shifts because the absent party's interest can be protected by shaping relief.

The accident occurred in Kansas on October 1, 1943; Ragan filed in the District of Kansas on September 4, 1945 and served the summons on December 28, 1945, after Kansas's two-year period; the district court denied summary judgment and a verdict was entered for Ragan, the Tenth Circuit reversed, and the Supreme Court affirmed in an opinion by Justice Douglas, with Justice Rutledge dissenting.

The Court's rationale was that a state-created cause of action cannot be given longer life in federal court than it would have in state court; Walker v. Armco Steel (1980) reaffirmed Ragan after Hanna, reading Rule 3 as not addressing tolling of state limitations periods.

The suit began when Planters Flying Service sued D.M. Barton in Arkansas for crop-spraying fees; Barton answered that the spraying had ruined his Missouri cotton crop and cross-complained against the insecticide's manufacturer, Reasor-Hill, which then petitioned the Arkansas Supreme Court for a writ to stop the trial court from hearing the cross-complaint.

The fund was a Merrill Lynch brokerage account (roughly $35 million) held by Arelma, S.A., a Panamanian company Marcos created; the Pimentel class of human-rights victims held a nearly $2 billion judgment against the Marcos estate and sought to attach the account, and Merrill Lynch filed the statutory interpleader naming the Republic, its Presidential Commission on Good Government, Arelma, PNB and the class.

Justice Kennedy wrote for the Court, reversing the Ninth Circuit, and Justices Stevens and Souter each concurred in part and dissented in part, preferring a remand rather than outright dismissal; the Court held that where a sovereign has a non-frivolous claim to the assets and sovereign immunity, dismissal is required under Rule 19(b) even though the claimants may be left without a forum.

Harris sued under § 1983 claiming an unreasonable Fourth Amendment seizure after Deputy Scott rammed his bumper during a roughly ten-mile high-speed chase in Georgia, leaving Harris a quadriplegic; the Court ruled 8-1 in an opinion by Justice Scalia, with Justices Ginsburg and Breyer concurring and Justice Stevens dissenting.

Rule statement: when opposing parties tell two different stories and one is blatantly contradicted by the record so that no reasonable jury could believe it, the court should not adopt that version of the facts in ruling on summary judgment; the Court also held that an officer's attempt to end a dangerous high-speed chase by forcing the fleeing motorist off the road does not violate the Fourth Amendment even at risk of serious injury to the motorist.

Shady Grove treated Sonia Galvez after a car accident and took an assignment of her Allstate benefits; Allstate paid late and refused the 2% statutory interest, worth about $500 to Shady Grove but roughly $5 million class-wide; N.Y. C.P.L.R. 901(b) bars class actions to recover statutory penalties, and the Eastern District of New York dismissed for lack of CAFA jurisdiction, with the Second Circuit affirming.

Justice Scalia's plurality asked only whether Rule 23 'really regulates procedure' (Sibbach), while Justice Stevens's controlling concurrence would hold a Federal Rule inapplicable where it would displace a state rule so intertwined with a state right or remedy that it functions to define the scope of the state-created right; Justice Ginsburg's dissent, joined by Justices Kennedy, Breyer and Alito, read Rule 23 and § 901(b) as not in conflict.

Heitner, a nonresident, brought a shareholder derivative suit against 28 present and former Greyhound officers and directors for conduct in Oregon, and used Delaware's sequestration statute to seize the stock and options of 21 of them; Justice Marshall wrote for the Court, Justice Powell concurred, Justice Stevens concurred in the judgment, Justice Brennan concurred in part and dissented in part, and Justice Rehnquist did not participate.

Rule statement: all assertions of state-court jurisdiction, including in rem and quasi in rem, must be evaluated under the International Shoe minimum-contacts standard; presence of property in the state is a relevant contact but, where the property is unrelated to the claim, it is not by itself sufficient.

Shamrock, a non-Texas corporation, sued Sheets (doing business as Friona Independent Oil Co.), a Texas citizen, in Texas state court on a verified account; Sheets counterclaimed for more than $3,000 for breach of a separate contract, and Chief Justice Stone wrote for a unanimous Court that the removal statute's reference to 'defendants' means only the defendants to the original action, so a plaintiff cannot remove on the basis of a counterclaim.

Shamrock is the standard citation for strict construction of removal jurisdiction: due regard for the rightful independence of state governments requires federal courts to scrupulously confine their jurisdiction to the precise limits the statute defines.

Rutter sued in federal court claiming superior title to a mining claim under the adverse-claim procedure of Revised Statutes §§ 2325-2326; the district court denied Shoshone's motion to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction and the court of appeals agreed, but the Supreme Court (7-1, Justice Brewer) reversed because the statutes let possession be decided by local customs, rules of miners and state law.

Sibbach was injured in Indiana and sued in federal court in Illinois, whose law did not allow court-ordered physical examinations; ordered to submit under Rule 35, she refused and was held in contempt under Rule 37, and the Seventh Circuit affirmed.

Although it upheld Rule 35, the Court (Justice Roberts, 5-4) actually reversed the contempt judgment because Rule 37 as then written did not authorize contempt for refusing a physical examination; Justice Frankfurter's dissent was joined by Justices Black, Douglas and Murphy. The majority's test, whether a rule 'really regulates procedure', is the language the Shady Grove plurality later adopted.

Smith sued in the Western District of Missouri to enjoin the company from investing in farm-loan bonds issued under the Federal Farm Loan Act of 1916; Missouri law allowed the trust company to invest only in securities authorized by valid law, so the state-law claim turned on the Act's constitutionality, which the Court (Justice Day) then upheld on the merits.

The underlying case was Hobson v. Hansen, in which Judge J. Skelly Wright found the D.C. schools' tracking system and other practices discriminated against black and poor children; the D.C. Circuit decided Smuck en banc in an opinion by Judge Bazelon, denying intervention to former superintendent Carl Hansen and dissenting board member Carl Smuck but allowing twenty parents to intervene and appeal only the decree provisions restricting the board's future discretion.

Family Finance claimed $420 on a promissory note and, under a Wisconsin statute, served a garnishment writ on Sniadach's employer freezing half her wages before any hearing; the Wisconsin Supreme Court upheld the procedure and the U.S. Supreme Court reversed 7-1 in an opinion by Justice Douglas, with Justice Harlan concurring and Justice Black dissenting.

The Court treated wages as a specialized type of property whose prejudgment garnishment may drive a wage-earning family to the wall, so absent extraordinary circumstances notice and a prior hearing are required.

Rule stated by the court: when a nonresident is "inveigled, enticed or induced, by fraud, trickery, artifice or wrongful device for which a party is responsible by virtue of the action of his attorney to come within the jurisdiction for the purpose of enabling such party to obtain personal service of process, service of process which results from such fraud, trickery, artifice or wrongful device is invalid and does not justify the exercise of jurisdiction by such court over the person so served with process."

Richard Tickle, a minor, sued Raymond Barton, a resident of Austinville, Virginia, in the Circuit Court of McDowell County for injuries inflicted by a motor vehicle on private property; Barton alleged that Tickle's attorney telephoned him and refused to identify himself when asked, while persuading him to attend a banquet in West Virginia.

The Supreme Court's decision was per curiam. Robert Tolan, unarmed, was shot on his parents' front porch by Sergeant Jeffrey Cotton on New Year's Eve 2008; the suit was under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for excessive force, and the summary-judgment ruling arose on the officer's qualified-immunity defense.

The Court faulted the Fifth Circuit for failing to adhere to the axiom that on summary judgment "[t]he evidence of the nonmovant is to be believed, and all justifiable inferences are to be drawn in his favor."

Justice Kavanaugh wrote for a 5–4 Court (Roberts, Alito, Gorsuch, Barrett joining); the opinion's rule is often reduced to "No concrete harm, no standing," and it held that only plaintiffs concretely harmed by a statutory violation may seek damages against a private defendant in federal court.

Justice Brennan wrote the opinion; the case came from the Eastern District of Tennessee, where a jury found for Gibbs, and the Sixth Circuit affirmed before the Supreme Court granted certiorari. The Court replaced the narrower Hurn v. Oursler test with the 'common nucleus of operative fact' standard, under which the state and federal claims must be ones a plaintiff would ordinarily expect to try in one judicial proceeding.

Despite upholding pendent jurisdiction, the Court reversed the judgment for Gibbs on the merits, so the case is a jurisdictional win and a substantive loss for the plaintiff; pendent jurisdiction was described as a doctrine of discretion, not of plaintiff's right, and state claims should ordinarily be dismissed if the federal claims drop out before trial.

D'Agostino sued Heyward and its surety, Maryland Casualty Company, under the Miller Act for payments due on the Navy barracks job at the New London submarine base; Heyward counterclaimed for overpayments and extra completion costs on both the Navy job and the private Stelma plant job in Stamford, and the Second Circuit affirmed the judgment.

The proposed class was about 1.5 million current and former female employees across roughly 3,400 stores; Justice Scalia wrote for a 5–4 majority on commonality, which "requires the plaintiff to demonstrate that the class members 'have suffered the same injury'" and that the common contention is "capable of classwide resolution."

Gina Fiore and Keith Gipson, professional gamblers, had about $97,000 seized by Walden, a Georgia officer working as a DEA agent at the Atlanta airport; the district court dismissed for lack of personal jurisdiction, the Ninth Circuit reversed, and the Supreme Court (Thomas, J., unanimous) reversed the Ninth Circuit.

Walker, an Oklahoma carpenter injured by a defective nail on August 22, 1975, filed in federal court on August 19, 1977 (three days before the two-year limit) but did not serve Armco until December 1, 1977, outside Oklahoma's 60-day service window; the district court dismissed, the Tenth Circuit affirmed, and the Supreme Court affirmed, holding Rule 3 was not sufficiently broad to control the issue and was not intended to toll state limitations periods.

Interstate Realty, a Tennessee corporation, sued a Mississippi resident for a broker's commission on the sale of Mississippi land while doing business in Mississippi without qualifying under its statute.

Justice White wrote for a 6–3 Court; Justice Brennan dissented alone, Justice Marshall dissented joined by Justice Blackmun (a retailer joining a national network can expect its product to cause injury elsewhere), and Justice Blackmun dissented separately (automobiles are inherently mobile). The Robinsons bought the Audi from Seaway in 1976 and were driving to Arizona in 1977 when another car struck them.

The often-quoted test is whether the defendant's conduct and connection with the forum are such that it should reasonably anticipate being haled into court there; the manufacturer (Audi) and importer (Volkswagen of America) did not contest Oklahoma jurisdiction, only the regional distributor and the retail dealer did.

Newhouse was met at the Miami airport by Wyman, a deputy sheriff who served him, and a photographer; the Florida claims were for money loaned, money advanced, and seduction under promise of marriage. The Second Circuit affirmed the dismissal of the New York action on the judgment, reasoning that jurisdiction obtained by fraud is treated as no jurisdiction, so the judgment was void and not entitled to enforcement in another state.

The collision was at Vandeventer Avenue and North Market Street in St. Louis; the petition alleged injuries to her "neck, back, spine and nervous system"; the rule stated is that special damages must be pleaded or shown to be the necessary result of the injuries already alleged.

Decided by the Western District of Pennsylvania; Zippo Dot Com was a California corporation running a USENET news service that registered zippo.com, zippo.net and zipponews.com, and Zippo Manufacturing sued for trademark dilution, infringement and false designation under the Lanham Act and state law. Two of the seven Pennsylvania access-provider agreements were with providers in the Western District.

117 F. 99 (9th Cir. 1902). The March 1900 contracts paid $50 for the season; a second group signed in April at $60 for the season plus two cents per salmon, and both groups joined the demand for $100 after arriving at Pyramid Harbor.

Judge Andrew Carter (S.D.N.Y.) decided the motion on February 26, 2026; besides denying arbitration, the court held the class-action waiver in the 2019 Terms unenforceable against users who transacted under the 2017 Terms, because merely posting the revised terms on the website, with no evidence that the arbitration provision was announced, gave insufficient notice.

29 N.Y.2d 124 (1971), decided July 6, 1971 by a 4-3 vote: Chief Judge Fuld wrote for the majority (Burke, Scileppi and Gibson concurring), and Judge Bergan's dissent was joined by Judges Breitel and Jasen.

The majority's test: economic duress exists where one party is forced to agree to a modification by a wrongful threat precluding the exercise of free will, such as a threat to withhold needed goods when the victim cannot obtain them from another source and an ordinary breach-of-contract action would be inadequate.

[1919] 2 K.B. 571 (C.A.), decided 25 June 1919. Atkin L.J. reasoned that agreements between spouses living in amity are presumed not to be intended to create legal relations, and that enforcing them would flood the courts; Warrington L.J. rested on the absence of any bargain by the wife, and Duke L.J. warned that enforcing such domestic promises would be a fruitful source of dissension.

257 Va. 121, 509 S.E.2d 499 (1999). The boat reached only 13 mph on delivery (about 17 mph after repairs) against the 30 mph shown in the prop matrixes; the trial court had awarded Crow $135,000 plus prejudgment interest, and the Supreme Court of Virginia reversed on the implied warranties of merchantability and fitness as well as on the express warranty.

215 F.3d 219 (2d Cir. 2000). OMT lacked the tax-exempt registration that would have avoided the federal excise tax, so Bayway paid it; the court joined the consensus of other jurisdictions that the party opposing an additional term bears the burden of proving material alteration, defined as surprise or hardship.

601 F.2d 609 (2d Cir. 1979), affirming 454 F. Supp. 258 (S.D.N.Y. 1978). The royalty ran from April 1972 to March 1978, and the two clauses at issue were the promise to use best efforts to promote and maintain a high volume of sales and the liquidated payment triggered if Falstaff substantially discontinued distribution under the Ballantine name.
